newsitem.title: USA: Louisiana judge rules breast implant trial will go on.
newsitem.headline: Louisiana judge rules breast implant trial will go on.

text.p: A state court judge on Thursday reversed herself and denied a defence request for a mistrial in the first class action silicone breast implant case to go to trial against Dow Chemical Co., court officials said.

On Wednesday, New Orleans District Court Judge Yada T. Magee ended the trial on the grounds of "prejudicial misconduct," because gestures and non-verbal communications made by a "very engaging" and "charismatic" plaintiff's attorney might have influenced the jury.
A few hours later, Magee said she would reconsider the mistrial ruling overnight and issue a decision on Thursday morning, Dawn Barrios, one of the plaintiff's attorneys said Wednesday.

Magee overturned her mistrial ruling after a poll of jurors showed they were not influenced by the actions of attorney Tom Pirtle, the judge's law clerk said. Testimony in the nearly four-month-long trial will continue on Monday.

"A lawyer cannot be penalised simply for being likeable," said Barrios, lead Louisiana counsel for the women suing Dow Chemical. "The jury clearly told Judge Magee that nothing in my colleague's manner would render them incapable of an impartial reading of the facts.
Dow Chemical said it would appeal the reversal of the mistrial ruling in a state appeals court.

The suit initially covered an estimated 14,000 women who received silicone breast implants, 1,700 of whom recieved implants manufactured by the now-bankrupt Dow Corning Inc., a joint venture of Dow Chemical and Corning Inc.

The case was pared down to focus on damages claimed against Dow Chemical by eight class representatives, with the remainder of the case concerning Dow Corning implant recipients transferred to a Michigan federal court at the urging of Midland, Mich.-based Dow Chemical.

The Louisiana suit claims that Dow Chemical is liable for health problems stemming from the implants because it allegedly tested silicone compounds in its laboratories for Dow Corning and withheld evidence that the implants could be harmful. Dow Corning was dismissed from the case because of bankruptcy proceedings.
Another part of the class action suit, the case against Bristol-Myers Squibb Co., another manufacturer, will be tried later.
